prohibited_recommendations: Do not delay surgical referral once a temporal-lobe tumor is identified.
Do not start an enzyme-inducing ASM (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, topiramate above 200 mg/day) while she relies on the combined oral contraceptive.
Do not start valproate: it is not first-line for focal epilepsy and, under the 2024 MHRA rules, is not started under 55 unless two specialists document that no alternative works.

avoided_actions.rationale: Afebrile, no meningism or immunosuppression, and back to baseline: there is no indication for lumbar puncture.
No murmur, exertional event or cardiac history, and the semiology is epileptic: echocardiography has no indication.
Olfactory aura, automatisms and postictal confusion make syncope unlikely and the ECG is normal: ambulatory cardiac monitoring has no indication.
Back to baseline with a normal examination, no head injury and no anticoagulation: emergency CT is not indicated, and the epilepsy-protocol MRI answers the structural question.
FDG-PET adds nothing to a first diagnosis with concordant MRI and EEG; it belongs to presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant epilepsy.

accepted: Focal epilepsy of right temporal lobe origin secondary to dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor (DNET) (focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizure)

differential.key_features: Also a low-grade epileptogenic glioneuronal tumor of the mesial temporal lobe; the multicystic, non-enhancing appearance without calcification favors DNET, and only histology separates them.

differential.key_features: Cortical dysplasia adjacent to a glioneuronal tumor is a histological diagnosis made after resection.
No hemorrhage, hemosiderin rim or blooming on susceptibility-weighted imaging.
Olfactory aura, automatisms and postictal confusion, with a normal ECG.

differential.diagnosis: Genetic generalized epilepsy (history of childhood absence epilepsy)
differential.key_features: Focal olfactory aura with automatisms, right temporal focal discharges without generalized spike-wave, and a right mesial temporal lesion argue against it.

key_clinical_evidence: Eight to ten stereotyped olfactory auras with nausea and dread over 14 months, some with impaired awareness, are prior focal seizures, so the two-seizure criterion for epilepsy is met [ILAE_def_2014].
Olfactory aura, oroalimentary and right manual automatisms, a right mesial temporal lesion and right anterior temporal discharges are concordant.
Epilepsy-protocol MRI is the central study; post-contrast images are added once a lesion is seen [ILAE_MRI_2019].
DNET is a CNS WHO grade 1 glioneuronal tumor; resection gives seizure freedom in most patients [Blumcke_2017].
Ethinylestradiol roughly halves lamotrigine levels [Sabers_2003], while enzyme-inducing ASMs make the combined pill unreliable.

general.query: focal epilepsy in adults: definition, classification, imaging and first-line treatment

results.finding: Epilepsy is present after at least two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, after one unprovoked seizure with a recurrence risk of at least 60% over the next 10 years, or when an epilepsy syndrome is diagnosed.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2014;55:475-482 | ILAE official report: a practical clinical definition of epilepsy

results.finding: Seizures are classified by onset as focal, generalized or unknown; focal seizures are described by awareness and by their first motor or non-motor feature, and may evolve to focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2017;58:522-530 | Operational classification of seizure types by the International League Against Epilepsy: position paper of the ILAE Commission for Classification and Terminology

results.finding: A harmonized epilepsy MRI protocol (3D T1 and 3D FLAIR at about 1 mm isotropic resolution and high-resolution coronal T2) is recommended for adults with focal epilepsy; non-dedicated protocols miss subtle lesions.
results.source: Bernasconi A et al., Epilepsia 2019;60:1054-1068 | Recommendations for the use of structural magnetic resonance imaging in the care of patients with epilepsy: a consensus report from the International League Against Epilepsy Neuroimaging Task Force

results.finding: Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is offered as first-line monotherapy for focal seizures, with carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, zonisamide or lacosamide as further options.
results.source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, NG217 2022 | Epilepsies in children, young people and adults

results.finding: Drug-resistant epilepsy is failure of adequate trials of two tolerated, appropriately chosen and used antiseizure medication schedules to achieve sustained seizure freedom.
results.source: Kwan P et al., Epilepsia 2010;51:1069-1077 | Definition of drug resistant epilepsy: consensus proposal by the ad hoc Task Force of the ILAE Commission on Therapeutic Strategies

general.summary: Epilepsy is diagnosed after two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart or one with a high recurrence risk, and focal seizures are classified by onset and awareness (ILAE 2014, 2017). A dedicated epilepsy-protocol MRI is the imaging of choice (ILAE 2019). Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is first-line monotherapy for focal seizures (NICE NG217), and drug resistance is failure of two appropriate medication schedules (ILAE 2010).

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Dominguez is a 27-year-old left-handed Hispanic female elementary school teacher who was brought to the emergency department by ambulance after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure during the school day. According to her teaching assistant who witnessed the event, the patient was standing at the front of the classroom when she suddenly stopped speaking mid-sentence, turned her head slowly to the right, and appeared to stare blankly. She then began making chewing and swallowing motions and picked at her blouse repeatedly with her right hand. After approximately 20 seconds, she collapsed to the floor and developed bilateral arm and leg stiffening followed by rhythmic jerking of all four extremities lasting approximately 70 seconds. She was placed on her side by staff. Paramedics arrived within 8 minutes and found her confused, disoriented, and unable to answer questions. By the time she reached the emergency department, approximately 45 minutes after the event, she was becoming more alert but remained drowsy and disoriented.

On interview, the patient reports that immediately before the episode she perceived a strong, unpleasant odor that she describes as resembling burning rubber. This was accompanied by an intense wave of nausea that rose from her abdomen. She felt a sense of unreality and dread, as though something terrible was about to happen. She has no memory of anything after the onset of the smell until she woke up in the ambulance. She reports that she has experienced identical episodes of the burning rubber smell accompanied by nausea and a feeling of dread approximately eight to ten times over the past fourteen months. These episodes previously lasted 30 to 90 seconds and resolved spontaneously, leaving her feeling briefly confused. On two occasions, coworkers commented that she seemed to zone out and was unresponsive for a short period, but she assumed she was simply daydreaming. She did not seek medical attention for these episodes. She denies any history of head trauma, meningitis, encephalitis, or prior seizures other than the childhood absence seizures that resolved spontaneously. She reports no recent illness, fever, or significant sleep deprivation. Her last menstrual period was two weeks ago. She has no recent medication changes.
